title: Larimer County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Larimer County wells have a 190 ft median depth and 6 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost, water table trends, and buyer risks.
h1: Water wells in Larimer County, Colorado
intro_html:
Larimer County covers a lot of different mountain settings, from the foothills around Fort Collins and Loveland up through Estes Park and Red Feather Lakes. Most wells here are in hard fractured bedrock, and the state records give a decent picture of how deep you’ll likely drill, how much water you can expect, and what that will cost.

Below is a plain‑language rundown of the Larimer County well numbers and what they mean if you’re buying land or planning to build on a well.

sections.heading: How deep Larimer County wells usually go
sections.html:
Across Larimer County, the median well depth is 190 feet, with the middle half running from 40 to 400 feet. About 39% of wells are under 100 feet, another 22% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 27% run 300 to 600 feet. Around 11% go beyond 600 feet, and the deepest on record hits 2,340 feet.

That spread is typical of fractured mountain bedrock. A driller bidding a new domestic well near places like Livermore, Drake, or Glen Haven is going to look hard at the nearby permits, but from the countywide numbers alone you should be financially prepared for something in the 200–400 foot range, knowing it could be less or a lot more on a specific parcel.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water to expect here
sections.html:
Out of 5,407 Larimer County wells that report a tested yield, the median is 6 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4 and 10 gpm. Only about 7% of wells come in under 1 gpm, 22% land between 1 and 5 gpm, 60% are in the 5 to 15 gpm band, and 12% report more than 15 gpm.

For a typical exempt household well, anything in the 4–10 gpm range is generally workable if the driller confirms it’s sustainable. The small share of sub‑1 gpm wells is a warning to check individual well permits around your property instead of relying only on county averages, especially in the rockier high country and more remote valleys.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trends in Larimer County
sections.html:
The county’s 1,058 static water level reports show a median depth to water of 50 feet, with the middle half between 15 and 100 feet below ground. That’s the distance from land surface down to the standing water in the well, not the total depth.

Looking by decade, the median depth to water has steadily increased: about 13 feet in the 1950s, 21–25 feet in the 1960s–1980s, 35 feet in the 1990s, 49 feet in the 2000s, 76 feet in the 2010s, and 80 feet so far in the 2020s. That pattern points to a general deepening water table over time. On a new build, figure on lifting water farther than older wells nearby do, which affects pump sizing and power use.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how active wells have been
sections.html:
Larimer County has 20,592 well permits on the books, with 12,847 recorded as constructed and 13,679 reporting a total depth. Permitting took off in the 1970s and 1980s, with 2,383 and 2,385 permits respectively, then climbed to 4,089 in the 1990s. Activity stayed strong in the 2000s with 3,010 permits, followed by 2,163 in the 2010s and 1,316 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit is from 2025.

Most wells are for domestic or household use (about 68%), with stock wells at 7%, irrigation around 5%, and monitoring wells about 15%. The bulk of the work has been done by drillers like Ingram Drilling Inc., Authorized (Pe, Pg), and Hersh & Son Well Drilling Inc., who collectively account for several thousand of the county’s wells.

sections.heading: What it costs to drill a new well in Larimer County
sections.html:
Most Larimer County wells are in fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss. Typical drilling here runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 190 foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself in roughly the $12,400–$19,000 range.

Once you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished median‑depth well usually falls around $18,400–$31,000. Deeper wells toward the 300–600 foot range common in some foothill and high‑country areas will scale up from there. When you budget, look at nearby well depths on state records and plan for the higher end rather than hoping to hit one of the shallow 40–100 foot holes.

sections.heading: Geology, contamination, and other local risks
sections.html:
Most permits list an unnamed fractured‑bedrock aquifer; 18,611 wells fall into that category. A smaller number tap alluvial sources, with 393 wells in Alluvial and 108 in Quaternary Alluvium. Fractured rock can be hit‑or‑miss on yield over short distances, which is why you see both strong producers and a 7% share under 1 gpm countywide.

Larimer County also has mapped environmental concerns: about 90 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, roughly 70 historic mine features, and around 40 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Before drilling or buying, it’s worth comparing your location to these mapped areas and planning for a thorough water test panel, not just basic bacteria and nitrate.

sections.heading: Buying or building on land with a well in Larimer County
sections.html:
With a 190 foot median depth, a 6 gpm median yield, and a water table that has deepened from roughly 13 feet in the 1950s to about 80 feet in the 2020s, Larimer County is workable but not casual when it comes to wells. Most wells are domestic, and the county has 5,407 with reported yields and 1,058 with static levels, so you usually can find nearby data.

For an existing home, pull the DWR permit, look at tested yield and construction details, and budget for pump replacement if the well is older. For vacant land, look at depths and yields of surrounding wells, confirm drilling access, and factor the full $18,400–$31,000 finished‑well cost into your build numbers before you commit.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Larimer County, Colorado?
faq.a: State records show a median Larimer County well depth of 190 feet, with the middle half between 40 and 400 feet. About 39% of wells are under 100 feet, while 27% fall between 300 and 600 feet and 11% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 2,340 feet. For a specific property, check nearby well permits rather than relying only on the countywide median.

faq.q: What is a good well yield in Larimer County, CO?
faq.a: Of the 5,407 Larimer County wells reporting a pump test, the median yield is 6 gpm and the middle half range is 4–10 gpm. Only about 7% test below 1 gpm, while 60% fall between 5 and 15 gpm and 12% exceed 15 gpm. For a typical household exempt well, a sustained yield around the 4–10 gpm band is usually adequate if the system is designed correctly.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Larimer County?
faq.a: The static water level records suggest a long-term deepening. Median depth to water was about 13 feet in the 1950s, rose into the low 20s by the 1970s–1980s, then to 35 feet in the 1990s, 49 feet in the 2000s, 76 feet in the 2010s, and about 80 feet in the 2020s. That trend means newer wells often need to lift water farther than older wells nearby, which affects pump sizing and operating cost.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Larimer County?
faq.a: In Larimer County’s fractured granite and gneiss, typical drilling runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the 190 foot county median depth, that’s roughly $12,400–$19,000 for the borehole. A complete system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical commonly totals around $18,400–$31,000 at that depth. Deeper wells toward the 300–600 foot range increase cost in a roughly linear way with added footage.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Larimer County, Colorado?
faq.a: The county has about 90 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, some 70 historic mine features, and roughly 40 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, plus mostly fractured‑bedrock aquifers. That mix means water quality can vary by location. Many households use their wells for drinking, but you should always test a well for bacteria, nitrate, and a broader panel if you’re near mining or known contamination areas.
